title: Continuous-time synthesis for Metric Interval Temporal Logic
formal: For the future-time MITL signal semantics below, is it decidable whether an input specification phi admits a causal operator F from finitely variable input signals to finitely variable output signals such that the combined signal (I,F(I)) satisfies phi at time zero for every input I?
definitions:
Input and output proposition sets are disjoint finite sets supplied with the formula. A signal maps the nonnegative reals to their Boolean valuations. Finite variability means there is an unbounded sequence 0=t_0<t_1<… on each open interval (t_i,t_{i+1}) of which the signal is constant. Values at the isolated boundary times are independent of either neighboring interval; right continuity is not imposed. No finite accumulation of change times is allowed.

The selected MITL syntax uses atoms, true, false, Boolean connectives and the future until operator U_J. J is an interval of nonnegative reals with rational finite endpoints or upper endpoint infinity, specified with open or closed finite endpoints, and with positive length; singleton intervals are forbidden. Rational endpoints are encoded in binary. For the joint signal s, (s,t) satisfies alpha U_J beta iff some t′>t has t′−t∈J, beta holds at t′, and alpha holds at every u with t<u<t′. Boolean operators have ordinary two-valued semantics. This strict-until convention and the exclusion of past operators are explicit editorial choices.

F is causal if I and I′ agreeing throughout [0,t] implies F(I)(t)=F(I′)(t) for every t. Thus it may react to the present input value but not future values. F is otherwise an arbitrary mathematical total operator; no finite-state, MSO-definability, computability or bounded-delay condition is imposed. The question is existence-decidability, not construction of a program in an unspecified implementation language.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked total decision procedure for the stated syntax and semantics, or a complete undecidability reduction preserving these conventions. A timed-word game result must be accompanied by an equivalence to this signal and causal-operator model. Merely deciding satisfiability of phi does not decide causal realizability.
context:
Rabinovich and Fattal decide continuous-time synthesis for MSO with order on finitely variable signals. Their conclusion asks about adding restricted metric specifications such as MITL.

They explicitly distinguish arbitrary causal operators from definable ones and distinguish signals from timed-word games. Those distinctions are retained in this variant.
why: The problem asks whether metric real-time specifications can be automatically realized as causal behavior.

import_provenance.original_title: Continuous-time synthesis for Metric Interval Temporal Logic
import_provenance.original_statement: Is the Church synthesis problem decidable for MITL specifications over finitely variable signals on the nonnegative real line? Given a specification relating input and output signals, determine whether a causal operator can satisfy it for every input, with output at time t depending only on input up to t.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: The authors settle MSO order specifications, not MITL’s metric constraints; this is their signal-operator synthesis model, rather than a differently parameterized timed-game model.

context_blocks.text: Rabinovich and Fattal decide continuous-time synthesis for MSO with order on finitely variable signals. Their conclusion asks about adding restricted metric specifications such as MITL.
They explicitly distinguish arbitrary causal operators from definable ones and distinguish signals from timed-word games. Those distinctions are retained in this variant.

sentences: Specifications describe Boolean signals indexed by continuous nonnegative time.
Metric until operators constrain delays using nonsingleton rational intervals.
The output may depend on the input up to and including the present instant.
The target is deciding existence of any causal implementation that preserves finite variability.
The editorial syntax and boundary conventions prevent conflating this with other timed-game models.
